cityPlaces.name: Hypogeum of Via Dino Compagni (Via Latina catacomb)
cityPlaces.summary: Private hypogeum of about 320-360 discovered in 1955, with over 100 paintings of Old Testament scenes and pagan myths side by side, including Hercules and Alcestis.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of Castulus
cityPlaces.summary: Catacomb of the martyr Castulus on the Via Labicana near the aqueduct arches.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of Cyriaca (San Lorenzo)
cityPlaces.summary: Cemetery around the tomb of St Lawrence (d. 258), over which Constantine built a funerary basilica and Pelagius II (579-590) a new church.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of Novatian
cityPlaces.summary: Catacomb found in 1932 with the epitaph of a martyr Novatian, probably the 3rd-century schismatic.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of Hippolytus
cityPlaces.summary: Cemetery of the theologian and martyr Hippolytus (d. c. 235) on the Via Tiburtina, with an underground basilica described by Prudentius.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of Nicomedes
cityPlaces.summary: Small catacomb of the martyr Nicomedes close to the Porta Nomentana.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Jewish catacomb of Villa Torlonia
cityPlaces.summary: Jewish catacomb of the late 2nd-4th centuries with painted menorahs and Torah shrines, among the earliest Jewish catacombs.
scholarship: Rutgers, The Jews in Late Ancient Rome (1995)
Noy, Jewish Inscriptions of Western Europe II: The City of Rome (1995)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Anonymous catacomb of Via dei Villini
cityPlaces.summary: Small anonymous Christian catacomb near the Porta Nomentana.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of Sant'Agnese
cityPlaces.summary: Cemetery around the tomb of the girl martyr Agnes, under the basilica built by Pope Honorius I (625-638) and beside Constantina's great funerary basilica.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Coemeterium Maius
cityPlaces.summary: One of the largest catacombs, with a painted orant Virgin and Child of the 4th century.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Coemeterium Minus (Ostrianum)
cityPlaces.summary: Smaller cemetery near the Coemeterium Maius, later associated with Peter's preaching.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of Felicitas (Maximus)
cityPlaces.summary: Cemetery of the martyr Felicitas and of Silanus, one of her sons, with a basilica restored by Boniface I.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of Thraso
cityPlaces.summary: Catacomb of the martyrs Saturninus and Sisinnius on land of a wealthy Christian named Thraso.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of the Giordani
cityPlaces.summary: Multi-level catacomb with 4th-century paintings, named after the martyr sons of Felicitas.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Anonymous catacomb of Via Anapo
cityPlaces.summary: Small catacomb found in 1921 with early 4th-century biblical paintings.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of Pamphilus
cityPlaces.summary: Catacomb on the Old Salaria with a well-preserved underground basilica of the martyr Pamphilus.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of Hermes and Bassilla
cityPlaces.summary: Cemetery with a large underground basilica of the martyr Hermes and the tomb of the virgin Bassilla.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb ad Clivum Cucumeris
cityPlaces.summary: Catacomb on the slope of the Clivus Cucumeris along the Old Salaria, rediscovered in the 20th century.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of San Valentino
cityPlaces.summary: Cemetery of the martyr Valentine on the Via Flaminia, with a basilica built by Julius I and restored in the 7th century.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Anonymous catacomb of Sant'Onofrio al Gianicolo
cityPlaces.summary: Small anonymous catacomb under the Janiculum by Sant'Onofrio.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Anonymous catacomb of Villa Pamphili
cityPlaces.summary: Catacomb in the grounds of Villa Doria Pamphili, with galleries cut from a 2nd-century hypogeum.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of Calepodius
cityPlaces.summary: Catacomb on the Via Aurelia where Pope Callixtus (d. 222) was buried, rediscovered in 1960.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of Processus and Martinianus
cityPlaces.summary: Cemetery of the two martyrs said to have been Peter's jailers, with a basilica restored in the 7th century.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of San Pancrazio (Octavilla)
cityPlaces.summary: Cemetery of the boy martyr Pancras on the Janiculum, under the basilica rebuilt by Honorius I (625-638).
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Catacomb of Pontianus
cityPlaces.summary: Catacomb on the Monteverde slope with a baptistery fed by a spring and 6th-7th century paintings of the martyrs Abdon and Sennen.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: Jewish catacomb of Monteverde
cityPlaces.summary: The oldest Jewish catacomb of Rome, serving the community of Trastevere from the 1st-2nd century; explored from 1602 and destroyed by quarrying in the 1920s.
scholarship: Rutgers, The Jews in Late Ancient Rome (1995)
Noy, Jewish Inscriptions of Western Europe II: The City of Rome (1995)
cityPlaces.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

cityPlaces.name: House of Valerius Publicola on the Velia
cityPlaces.summary: When the people suspected that the consul Valerius was building a fortress-like house on the summit of the Velia above the Forum, he had it pulled down overnight and rebuilt at the foot of the hill, earning the name Publicola.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of Spurius Cassius
cityPlaces.summary: The house of the consul Spurius Cassius, executed in 485 BC for aiming at kingship, was razed; the Temple of Tellus later rose on the empty site on the Carinae.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of Spurius Maelius (Aequimaelium)
cityPlaces.summary: Maelius, a rich knight who sold grain cheaply during a famine, was killed in 439 BC as a would-be tyrant; his house was demolished and the empty plot below the Capitol was called the Aequimaelium.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of Marcus Manlius Capitolinus on the Arx
cityPlaces.summary: The saviour of the Capitol from the Gauls lived on the Arx; after his execution in 384 BC his house was razed and patricians were forbidden to live on the Capitol. The Temple of Juno Moneta was later built on the site.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of Vitruvius Vaccus (Prata Vacci)
cityPlaces.summary: The house on the Palatine of Vitruvius Vaccus of Fundi, executed after his revolt in 330 BC, was razed and the site left open as the 'meadows of Vaccus'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of Scipio Africanus
cityPlaces.summary: Scipio Africanus lived behind the Tabernae Veteres near the statue of Vortumnus; in 169 BC Ti. Sempronius Gracchus bought the house and the shops behind it to build the Basilica Sempronia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of M. Fulvius Flaccus (Porticus Catuli)
cityPlaces.summary: The house on the Palatine of Fulvius Flaccus, killed with Gaius Gracchus in 121 BC, was razed; Q. Lutatius Catulus built a portico on the site with spoils from the Cimbric war, which Clodius later tried to merge into his shrine of Libertas.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of Gaius Gracchus
cityPlaces.summary: Gaius Gracchus moved from his house on the Palatine to the district below the Forum where the poor and humble lived, to show himself a man of the people.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
cityPlaces.note: Precise district unknown; placed between the Forum and the Subura.

cityPlaces.name: House of L. Licinius Crassus the orator
cityPlaces.summary: The orator Crassus (cos. 95 BC) shocked contemporaries with six columns of Hymettian marble in his Palatine house and famous lotus trees in its garden; the censor Ahenobarbus mocked him as the 'Palatine Venus'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of Cicero on the Palatine
cityPlaces.summary: Cicero bought the house of M. Livius Drusus on the north slope of the Palatine above the Forum from Crassus in 62 BC for 3.5 million sesterces. Clodius burned it during Cicero's exile in 58 and built a shrine of Libertas on part of the site; the Senate restored the land in 57 and Cicero rebuilt.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

phases.t: burned by Clodius; shrine of Libertas

cityPlaces.note: Located by its view over the Forum; remains under the Domus Tiberiana's north-east slope have been proposed.

cityPlaces.name: House of Clodius on the Palatine
cityPlaces.summary: Clodius bought the neighbouring house of Scaurus for 14.8 million sesterces, intending to join it to Cicero's former site, before his death on the Via Appia in 52 BC.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of M. Aemilius Scaurus
cityPlaces.summary: The aedile of 58 BC moved the 38-foot marble columns of his temporary theatre into the atrium of his house on the Palatine slope below the Sacra Via. Carandini's excavations identified a large atrium house at the north-east foot of the Palatine as Scaurus'.
scholarship: Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
Carandini and Carafa, Palatium e Sacra Via I (1995)

cityPlaces.name: House of Pompey on the Carinae
cityPlaces.summary: Pompey's ancestral, modest house on the Carinae, decorated with ships' beaks. After his death Mark Antony took it and Cicero mocked him for it; Tiberius later lived there before moving to the Gardens of Maecenas.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of Caesar in the Subura
cityPlaces.summary: Before his election as pontifex maximus in 63 BC, when he moved into the Domus Publica on the Sacra Via, Caesar lived in a modest house in the Subura.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
cityPlaces.note: Exact site unknown.

cityPlaces.name: House of Atticus (Domus Tamphiliana)
cityPlaces.summary: Cicero's friend Atticus lived on the Quirinal in the Tamphilian house he inherited from his uncle, more charming for its grove than its buildings.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
cityPlaces.note: Near the Temple of Quirinus and the Temple of Salus.

cityPlaces.name: Birthplace of Augustus 'ad Capita Bubula'
cityPlaces.summary: Augustus was born in September 63 BC in a house at the 'Ox-heads' at the north-east corner of the Palatine, later made a shrine.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of Agrippa and Messalla on the Palatine
cityPlaces.summary: Augustus gave the former house of Mark Antony on the Palatine jointly to Agrippa and Valerius Messalla after it burned.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House and tower of Maecenas
cityPlaces.summary: Maecenas built his mansion with a high tower on the Esquiline over the filled-in necropolis; Horace invites the reader to look down from it on the smoke and wealth of Rome, and Nero watched the Great Fire from the 'tower of Maecenas'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of Virgil on the Esquiline
cityPlaces.summary: Virgil had a house on the Esquiline next to the gardens of Maecenas.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
cityPlaces.note: Exact site unknown.

cityPlaces.name: House of Ovid near the Capitol
cityPlaces.summary: In the poem on his last night in Rome Ovid looks out at the Capitol, the temple 'near our house'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of the Laterani
cityPlaces.summary: Mansion on the Caelian of Plautius Lateranus, consul-designate executed in the Pisonian conspiracy of 65; confiscated, it passed to the emperors and gave its name to the Lateran. Remains lie under the Lateran hospital.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

cityPlaces.name: House of the Flavii 'ad Malum Punicum'
cityPlaces.summary: Domitian was born in 51 in his father Vespasian's house on the Quirinal at the 'Pomegranate'; he later turned it into the Templum Gentis Flaviae, the family mausoleum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: Flat of Martial 'ad Pirum'
cityPlaces.summary: Martial lived on the Quirinal near the 'Pear Tree', up three high flights of stairs, before he acquired a small house and returned to Spain in 98.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of Pliny the Younger on the Esquiline
cityPlaces.summary: Pliny's town house stood on the Esquiline near the Lacus Orphei, at the top of the slope beyond the Subura; Martial sends his book there.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of Licinius Sura
cityPlaces.summary: Trajan's marshal L. Licinius Sura had a house on the Aventine beside his baths overlooking the Circus Maximus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
cityPlaces.note: Next to the Balneum Surae.

cityPlaces.name: Privata Traiani (Trajan's private house)
cityPlaces.summary: Trajan's house before his accession, listed in Region XIII on the Aventine. The house with fine paintings under Santa Prisca has been proposed.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: House of Annius Verus (birthplace of Marcus Aurelius)
cityPlaces.summary: Marcus Aurelius was born in 121 in the gardens of his family on the Caelian near the house of Lateranus, where an equestrian statue, perhaps the Capitoline one, later stood.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: Domus Vectiliana
cityPlaces.summary: House on the Caelian to which Commodus moved, saying he could not sleep in the palace; he was strangled there on 31 December 192.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: Domus Cilonis
cityPlaces.summary: Mansion of L. Fabius Cilo, urban prefect and friend of Septimius Severus, listed in Region XII on the Piccolo Aventino; remains are associated with Santa Balbina.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Domus Cilonis
Guidobaldi, 'Le domus tardoantiche di Roma', in Lavan and Bowden (eds), Theory and Practice in Late Antique Archaeology (2003)

cityPlaces.name: House of the Tetrici
cityPlaces.summary: After his surrender to Aurelian the Gallic emperor Tetricus lived in Rome in a fine house on the Caelian 'between the two groves opposite the Temple of Isis Metellina', with a mosaic showing Aurelian investing him.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: Domus Faustae (Lateran)
cityPlaces.summary: The house of the empress Fausta at the Lateran, where Pope Miltiades held the synod of October 313 against the Donatists.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

cityPlaces.name: House of Symmachus on the Caelian
cityPlaces.summary: Town house on the Caelian of Q. Aurelius Symmachus, urban prefect and orator, leader of the pagan senators in the Altar of Victory affair; inscriptions honouring the family were found on the hill.
scholarship: Guidobaldi, 'Le domus tardoantiche di Roma', in Lavan and Bowden (eds), Theory and Practice in Late Antique Archaeology (2003)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
cityPlaces.note: His house in Trastevere was attacked by a mob in a grain shortage.

cityPlaces.name: Domus Valeriorum (Melania and Pinianus)
cityPlaces.summary: Palatial house of the Valerii on the Caelian near Santo Stefano Rotondo. Melania the Younger and Pinianus tried to sell it to give the money to the poor, but no one in Rome could afford it; after the sack of 410 it was sold cheaply. Parts with bronze patronage tablets were found in 1554 and 1902.
scholarship: Guidobaldi, 'Le domus tardoantiche di Roma', in Lavan and Bowden (eds), Theory and Practice in Late Antique Archaeology (2003)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
cityPlaces.note: Identical with the 'house of Valerius' and 'house of Melania' on the Caelian; later the xenodochium Valerii.

cityPlaces.name: Domus Gaudentii
cityPlaces.summary: Late-antique house on the Caelian known from an inscription naming Gaudentius, one of the aristocratic mansions that covered the hill in the 4th century.
scholarship: Guidobaldi, 'Le domus tardoantiche di Roma', in Lavan and Bowden (eds), Theory and Practice in Late Antique Archaeology (2003)

cityPlaces.name: House of Marcella on the Aventine
cityPlaces.summary: The widow Marcella turned her Aventine house into a centre of ascetic study where Jerome taught. When the Goths entered in 410 they beat her to make her reveal hidden gold; she died soon after at St Paul's.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)

cityPlaces.name: Case Romane del Celio (house of Pammachius)
cityPlaces.summary: A 2nd-century apartment block with shops on the Clivus Scauri, joined in the 3rd-4th centuries into one rich house with painted rooms and a small Christian confessio. Pammachius built the basilica of Santi Giovanni e Paolo over it around 410.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Guidobaldi, 'Le domus tardoantiche di Roma', in Lavan and Bowden (eds), Theory and Practice in Late Antique Archaeology (2003)

cityPlaces.name: Domus Pinciana (palace on the Pincian)
cityPlaces.summary: Great late-antique house on the Pincian, by the Aurelian Wall, perhaps of the Anicii Probi; Belisarius made it his headquarters during the Gothic siege of 537-538, and Pope Silverius was summoned and deposed there.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Guidobaldi, 'Le domus tardoantiche di Roma', in Lavan and Bowden (eds), Theory and Practice in Late Antique Archaeology (2003)

cityPlaces.name: Family house of Gregory the Great (Clivus Scauri)
cityPlaces.summary: The house of Gregory's family, of senatorial rank, on the Clivus Scauri facing the Palatine, which he converted into the monastery of St Andrew around 575.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)

cityPlaces.name: Domus under Palazzo Valentini
cityPlaces.summary: Two aristocratic houses of the 2nd-4th centuries with baths, mosaics and polychrome marble floors excavated under Palazzo Valentini near Trajan's Column, now a museum.
scholarship: Baldassarri (ed.), Palazzo Valentini: l'area archeologica (2008)

cityPlaces.name: House of Pudens (tradition)
cityPlaces.summary: Tradition held that the senator Pudens hosted Peter in his house on the Vicus Patricius; the 2nd-century bath and house remains below Santa Pudenziana gave rise to the story.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
cityPlaces.note: Legendary attribution.
